# Choose a string metric {#sec-uc-metrics}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_setup.R")
```

This package ships around thirty ways to score how alike two strings are.
Picking one by reputation -- "Jaro-Winkler is the standard for names" --
leaves the obvious question unanswered: standard for *which* names, against
*which* wrong answers?

This chapter answers it by measurement. Three hand-labelled sets of pairs,
one each for **given names**, **surnames** and **addresses**, are scored by
every candidate comparator, and the results say which comparator separates
the true pairs from the false ones in each field. Every number below is
computed when this page is rendered; the code is all here, so the same
exercise runs on your own labelled pairs by swapping the data in.

Three things fall out of it, and they are worth stating before the tables:

1. **The field matters more than the metric's reputation.** The comparator
   that wins on addresses is near the bottom on given names, and vice versa.
2. **Jaro-Winkler's prefix bonus is a liability when the wrong answers
   share a prefix** -- `ALAN`/`ALANA`, `HARRIS`/`HARRISON`,
   `12 SMITH ST`/`12 SMITH AVE`. Plain Jaro, or a length-sensitive edit
   similarity, discriminates better on exactly the pairs that cause
   trouble.
3. **For the hardest pairs no comparator works**, because the strings do not
   carry the answer: `BOB` and `ROBERT` are the same person and
   `SIMON` and `SIMONE` are not, and no function of two character vectors
   can know that. Those pairs are fixed by standardising before scoring, by
   comparing parsed components, or by another field -- never by a better
   metric. @sec-recipe does all three.

## The candidates

| Comparator | Call | What it rewards |
|---|---|---|
| Jaro-Winkler | `jaro_winkler(a, b)` | character agreement, with a bonus for a shared prefix |
| Jaro | `jaro_winkler(a, b, p = 0)` | the same, with no prefix bonus |
| Jaro-Winkler, tokens | `jaro_winkler_tokens(a, b)` | the best alignment of whole words, in any order |
| Monge-Elkan | `monge_elkan(a, b, symmetric = TRUE)` | each word's best match in the other string |
| Levenshtein | `levenshtein_similarity(a, b)` | few insertions, deletions, substitutions, relative to length |
| OSA | `osa_similarity(a, b)` | the same, counting an adjacent swap as one edit |
| Editex | `editex_similarity(a, b)` | edits, charging less for letters that sound alike |
| Indel | `indel_similarity(a, b)` | insertions and deletions only (no substitutions) |
| LCS (subsequence) | `lcs_seq_similarity(a, b)` | a long common subsequence |
| LCS (substring) | `lcs_str_similarity(a, b)` | one long *contiguous* run in common |
| Prefix | `prefix_similarity(a, b)` | a long common start |
| Smith-Waterman | `smith_waterman(a, b)` | the best-matching local region, gaps forgiven |
| Jaccard, 2-grams | `jaccard_index(a, b, q = 2)` | shared character pairs, penalising unshared ones |
| Jaccard, 3-grams | `jaccard_index(a, b, q = 3)` | the same, over longer and so more specific grams |
| Cosine, 3-grams | `cosine_similarity(a, b, q = 3)` | shared 3-grams, weighted by how often each occurs |
| Tversky containment | `tversky_index(a, b, q = 3, alpha = 1, beta = 0)` | how much of `a` appears in `b`, ignoring extra material in `b` |
| Token set | `fuzz_token_set_ratio(a, b)` | the words in common, ignoring order and duplicates |
| Weighted ratio | `fuzz_wratio(a, b)` | RapidFuzz's own blend of ratio, partial and token scorers |
| Soundex agreement | `soundex(a) == soundex(b)` | the same phonetic code -- a blocking key, included for contrast |

```{r}
#| label: comparators
comparators <- list(
    jaro_winkler   = function(a, b) jaro_winkler(a, b),
    jaro           = function(a, b) jaro_winkler(a, b, p = 0),
    jw_tokens      = function(a, b) jaro_winkler_tokens(a, b),
    monge_elkan    = function(a, b) monge_elkan(a, b, symmetric = TRUE),
    levenshtein    = function(a, b) levenshtein_similarity(a, b),
    osa            = function(a, b) osa_similarity(a, b),
    editex         = function(a, b) editex_similarity(a, b),
    indel          = function(a, b) indel_similarity(a, b),
    lcs_seq        = function(a, b) lcs_seq_similarity(a, b),
    lcs_str        = function(a, b) lcs_str_similarity(a, b),
    prefix         = function(a, b) prefix_similarity(a, b),
    smith_waterman = function(a, b) smith_waterman(a, b),
    jaccard_q2     = function(a, b) jaccard_index(a, b, q = 2),
    jaccard_q3     = function(a, b) jaccard_index(a, b, q = 3),
    cosine_q3      = function(a, b) cosine_similarity(a, b, q = 3),
    tversky_in     = function(a, b) tversky_index(a, b, q = 3, alpha = 1, beta = 0),
    fuzz_token_set = function(a, b) fuzz_token_set_ratio(a, b) / 100,
    fuzz_wratio    = function(a, b) fuzz_wratio(a, b) / 100,
    soundex_equal  = function(a, b) as.numeric(soundex(a) == soundex(b))
)
```

Every one is put on the same scale, where **1 means identical**: the
`*_similarity()` functions already are, the RapidFuzz scorers are divided
by 100, and distances are left out in favour of their similarity twins.
`rLink()` does this conversion itself, so a comparator chosen here drops
straight into a linkage (@sec-uc-link).

## The test pairs, graded by difficulty

A comparison is only as good as what it is compared against. Scoring true
matches against *randomly chosen* non-matches flatters every metric: every
comparator in the list separates `SMITH`/`SMYTH` from `SMITH`/`NGUYEN`.
What distinguishes them is the awkward middle, so each set grades both
classes:

| | easy | moderate | hard |
|---|---|---|---|
| **match** | one keystroke, a transposition, a dropped letter | a phonetic variant, a prefix convention, an abbreviation | a nickname, a short form, reordered or extra words |
| **non-match** | unrelated values | the same root word, a different locality | one decisive letter or digit apart |

```{r}
#| label: pairs-given
```

```{r}
12 SMITH ST,UNIT 4 12 SMITH ST ANNERLEY QLD 4103,extra detail,hard,TRUE

PO BOX 123 BRISBANE,41 MARINE PARADE REDCLIFFE,unrelated,easy,FALSE

12 SMITH ST BRISBANE,12 SMITH ST SYDNEY,different locality,moderate,FALSE

', stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

for (nm in c("given", "surname", "address")) {
    d <- get(nm)
    d$match <- as.logical(d$match)
    d$degree <- factor(d$degree, levels = c("easy", "moderate", "hard"))
    assign(nm, d)
}
```

The labels encode one judgement: *would a reviewer, seeing only this field,
call these the same person or address?* Several pairs are genuinely
arguable -- `THOMSON`/`THOMPSON` is a misspelling as often as it is two
families -- and they are labelled non-match deliberately, because a
comparator that cannot be told to be cautious there is a comparator that
will merge two people. The non-match side is adversarial by design: half of
it is near misses, where a real linkage would see mostly unrelated pairs.
The absolute numbers below are therefore pessimistic; what they are good for
is **ranking the comparators against each other** on the pairs that decide
a linkage.

## How each comparator is scored

Two measures, both reported per field:

- **AUC** -- the probability that a randomly chosen true pair outranks a
  randomly chosen false one, over the easy and moderate pairs only. It needs
  no threshold, which matters because the right threshold differs per
  comparator. The hard pairs are excluded here and reported separately,
  since (as the tables show) no comparator separates them and including
  them only compresses the ranking.
- **Mean score per cell** of the match x degree grid, which is where the
  behaviour actually shows: a comparator is useful when its moderate
  *matches* sit well above its moderate *non-matches*.

```{r}
#| label: scoring
score_all <- function(pairs) {
    scores <- lapply(comparators, function(f) f(pairs$a, pairs$b))
    cbind(pairs, as.data.frame(scores))
}

# Mann-Whitney / rank formulation: no bootstrapping, no ties problem
auc <- function(score, match) {
    r <- rank(score)
    n1 <- sum(match)
    n0 <- sum(!match)
    (sum(r[match]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

report <- function(pairs) {
    scored <- score_all(pairs)
    easy_mod <- scored$degree != "hard"
    cell <- function(v, keep) round(mean(v[keep]), 2)
    out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(comparators), function(nm) {
        v <- scored[[nm]]
        data.frame(
            comparator = nm,
            auc = round(auc(v[easy_mod], scored$match[easy_mod]), 2),
            tp_easy = cell(v, scored$match & scored$degree == "easy"),
            tp_mod  = cell(v, scored$match & scored$degree == "moderate"),
            tp_hard = cell(v, scored$match & scored$degree == "hard"),
            fp_easy = cell(v, !scored$match & scored$degree == "easy"),
            fp_mod  = cell(v, !scored$match & scored$degree == "moderate"),
            fp_hard = cell(v, !scored$match & scored$degree == "hard")
        )
    }))
    out$margin <- out$tp_mod - out$fp_mod
    out[order(-out$auc, -out$margin), ]
}

kable_report <- function(pairs, caption) {
    knitr::kable(
        report(pairs), row.names = FALSE, caption = caption,
        col.names = c("Comparator", "AUC", "easy", "moderate", "hard",
                      "easy", "moderate", "hard", "margin")
    )
}
```

In the tables, the first group of three columns is the mean score on **true
matches** of each difficulty, the second group the mean on **non-matches**,
and `margin` is the moderate gap between them -- the headroom a threshold
has to work in.

## Given names {#sec-given}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-given
#| tbl-cap: "Given names: 20 matched and 20 non-matched pairs. AUC over the easy and moderate pairs."
kable_report(given, NULL)
```

The ordering is emphatic, and it is the opposite of the folklore. The
length-sensitive edit similarities -- `levenshtein_similarity()`,
`osa_similarity()`, `lcs_seq_similarity()` -- separate these names almost
perfectly, while `jaro_winkler()` lands tenth of nineteen with a *negative*
margin: its moderate non-matches score **higher** (0.89) than its moderate
matches (0.88).

The reason is in the `prefix` row, and in the data. Every moderate
non-match here (`JOHN`/`JOHNATHAN`, `KIM`/`KIMBERLEY`, `SAM`/`SAMUEL`) is a
longer name that starts with the shorter one, and most of the hard
non-matches (`ALAN`/`ALANA`, `SIMON`/`SIMONE`, `MARTIN`/`MARTINA`) are the
same thing with one letter. Jaro-Winkler is built to reward a shared
prefix, so it rewards precisely the wrong pairs. Turning the bonus off
recovers much of the loss:

```{r}
#| label: prefix-bonus
confusable <- data.frame(
    a = c("ALAN", "SIMON", "MARTIN", "JOHN", "KIM", "DANIEL"),
    b = c("ALANA", "SIMONE", "MARTINA", "JOHNATHAN", "KIMBERLEY", "DANIELLE")
)
data.frame(
    confusable,
    jaro_winkler = round(jaro_winkler(confusable$a, confusable$b), 2),
    jaro         = round(jaro_winkler(confusable$a, confusable$b, p = 0), 2),
    osa          = round(osa_similarity(confusable$a, confusable$b), 2)
)
```

`p` is tunable rather than all-or-nothing: `0` gives plain Jaro, `0.25` the
maximum bonus. If your true matches are typos near the *start* of the
string -- common with scanned or dictated data -- keep the bonus. If your
hard non-matches are suffix extensions, as above, drop it.

The easy column shows what *is* uncontroversial: every comparator in the
table scores an easy match above 0.4 and an unrelated pair below 0.2, so for
clean data with only keystroke noise the choice hardly matters. It starts
mattering at `tp_mod`, and by `tp_hard` the question has changed entirely.

### What no comparator can do

Look along the hard row. The best `tp_hard` figures belong to comparators
that also score hard non-matches high, which is no use. The honest reading
is that the hard matches here are not a string problem at all:

```{r}
#| label: semantic
semantic <- given[given$degree == "hard" & given$match, c("a", "b", "kind")]
data.frame(
    semantic,
    jaro_winkler = round(jaro_winkler(semantic$a, semantic$b), 2),
    osa          = round(osa_similarity(semantic$a, semantic$b), 2),
    jw_tokens    = round(jaro_winkler_tokens(semantic$a, semantic$b), 2)
)
```

`BOB` is not a corrupted `ROBERT` and `PEGGY` is not a corrupted
`MARGARET`; they are different words for the same person. The fix is a
lookup, not a metric. `freplace_tokens()` applies a nickname table to whole
words in one vectorised pass, and the scores stop being a judgement call:

```{r}
#| label: nickname-table
nicknames <- c(
    BOB = "ROBERT", BILL = "WILLIAM", LIZ = "ELIZABETH", BETH = "ELIZABETH",
    PEGGY = "MARGARET", ALEX = "ALEXANDER", CHRIS = "CHRISTOPHER",
    SAM = "SAMANTHA", JIM = "JAMES"
)
standardised <- freplace_tokens(semantic$b, names(nicknames), nicknames)
data.frame(
    semantic["a"], b = semantic$b, standardised,
    before = round(jaro_winkler(semantic$a, semantic$b), 2),
    after  = round(jaro_winkler(semantic$a, standardised), 2)
)
```

The one row that stays low is `MARY JANE`/`JANE MARY`, which is not a
vocabulary problem but a word-order one -- and that is a metric choice after
all: `jaro_winkler_tokens()` scores it 1, as the table above shows. A
nickname table also has a cost: `SAM = "SAMANTHA"` fixes one row here and
would wrongly merge `SAM`/`SAMUEL`, so the table belongs with the rest of
your standardisation rules, under review, not buried in a scoring call.

## Surnames {#sec-surname}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-surname
#| tbl-cap: "Surnames: 16 matched and 18 non-matched pairs. AUC over the easy and moderate pairs."
kable_report(surname, NULL)
```

`osa_similarity()` and `lcs_seq_similarity()` lead again, but the
interesting rows are the next two.

**`editex_similarity()`** is the only comparator whose moderate matches
(0.84) beat its easy ones (0.83), because the moderate band is where the
phonetic variants live. It charges less for a substitution between letters
that sound alike, which is exactly the error surnames collect when they are
taken down by ear:

```{r}
#| label: editex-vs-lev
phonetic <- surname[surname$kind %in% c("phonetic", "prefix variant") &
                    surname$match, c("a", "b")]
data.frame(
    phonetic,
    levenshtein = round(levenshtein_similarity(phonetic$a, phonetic$b), 2),
    editex      = round(editex_similarity(phonetic$a, phonetic$b), 2)
)
```

**`soundex_equal`** -- phonetic-code agreement, not a similarity at all --
has the largest margin in the table (0.60) and perfect recall on the easy
and moderate matches. That is a real result, and a trap. It is 0 on every
hard match and 0.62 on the hard non-matches, because Soundex is built to
merge:

```{r}
#| label: soundex-hard
hard_fp <- surname[surname$degree == "hard" & !surname$match, c("a", "b")]
data.frame(
    hard_fp,
    code_a = soundex(hard_fp$a),
    code_b = soundex(hard_fp$b),
    same   = soundex(hard_fp$a) == soundex(hard_fp$b)
)
```

`CHAN`/`CHEN`, `WANG`/`WONG` and `HALL`/`HILL` all collapse to one code.
That makes phonetic codes excellent **blocking keys** -- generous, cheap,
and they bring the right pairs into consideration -- and poor deciders.
@sec-uc-link compares the codes by how aggressively they merge; use one to
generate candidates and a similarity to score them.

The hard matches here are the other familiar surname problem:
`SMITH`/`SMITH-JONES` after a marriage, `LEE`/`LEE NGUYEN`,
`VAN DER BERG`/`BERG`. One string is contained in the other, which is a
containment question, and the containment-shaped comparators answer it:

```{r}
#| label: containment-surnames
contained <- surname[surname$degree == "hard" & surname$match, c("a", "b")]
data.frame(
    contained,
    osa            = round(osa_similarity(contained$a, contained$b), 2),
    tversky_in     = round(tversky_index(contained$a, contained$b, q = 3,
                                         alpha = 1, beta = 0), 2),
    fuzz_token_set = round(fuzz_token_set_ratio(contained$a, contained$b) / 100, 2),
    smith_waterman = round(smith_waterman(contained$a, contained$b), 2)
)
```

`tversky_index(alpha = 1, beta = 0)` asks only "how much of `a` is in `b`?"
and so ignores the words `b` has added. Note that this makes it
**directional**, which the `VAN DER BERG`/`BERG` row shows: the extra words
are on the `a` side there, and the score collapses to 0.20. When either
side may be the fuller one -- which is the normal case across two files --
score both directions and keep the larger:

```{r}
#| label: containment-direction
both_ways <- pmax(
    tversky_index(contained$a, contained$b, q = 3, alpha = 1, beta = 0),
    tversky_index(contained$b, contained$a, q = 3, alpha = 1, beta = 0)
)
data.frame(contained, containment = round(both_ways, 2))
```

Containment costs precision: `tversky_in` is near the bottom of
@tbl-surname overall, because it also rates `MARTIN`/`MARTIN JR` and
`SINGH`/`SINGHA` highly -- which is the whole trade in one row. So score
both: a high `osa_similarity()` *or* a high containment score, with the
reason recorded, beats one blended number nobody can audit.

## Addresses {#sec-address}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-address
#| tbl-cap: "Addresses: 12 matched and 13 non-matched pairs. AUC over the easy and moderate pairs."
kable_report(address, NULL)
```

The ranking inverts. The q-gram set metrics and the containment score lead;
`jaro_winkler()` is second from last, and the edit similarities that won on
names are mid-table. Addresses break the assumptions those metrics make:

- **Length varies enormously** between two renderings of the same address
  (`9 KING ST` versus `9 KING STREET WEST END BRISBANE QUEENSLAND`). An
  edit similarity divides by the longer length, so a true match is punished
  for the detail one side happens to carry. `tversky_in` scores those pairs
  1.00 (`tp_hard`) precisely because it does not.
- **The decisive difference is tiny.** `12 SMITH ST` versus `21 SMITH ST`
  is two characters out of eleven, and a different house. Every comparator
  in the table scores the hard non-matches above 0.4, and the four best
  separators score them 0.69--0.84. There is no threshold that keeps those
  out.
- **Tokens move.** `LEVEL 3 100 QUEEN ST` and `100 QUEEN ST LEVEL 3` are
  one address, which rewards the token and q-gram comparators and penalises
  anything positional, `prefix_similarity()` worst of all (0.11 on moderate
  matches).

So the first thing to do with an address is not to pick a better
comparator; it is to stop comparing the whole string. Two moves fix most of
it. **Standardise** the vocabulary, then **compare components separately**,
exactly where an exact comparison belongs:

```{r}
#| label: address-components
street_types <- c(
    STREET = "ST", ROAD = "RD", AVENUE = "AVE", CRESCENT = "CRES",
    PARADE = "PDE", DRIVE = "DR", COURT = "CT", PLACE = "PL",
    HIGHWAY = "HWY", LANE = "LN", TERRACE = "TCE", SAINT = "ST"
)
std_address <- function(x) {
    freplace_tokens(fsquish(fupper(ascii_fold(x))),
                    names(street_types), street_types)
}
house_number <- function(x) fextract("^[0-9]+[A-Z]?", fsquish(fupper(x)))

hard_cases <- address[address$degree == "hard", ]
data.frame(
    hard_cases[c("a", "b", "match")],
    no_a  = house_number(hard_cases$a),
    no_b  = house_number(hard_cases$b),
    agree = house_number(hard_cases$a) == house_number(hard_cases$b),
    tversky_in = round(tversky_index(std_address(hard_cases$a),
                                     std_address(hard_cases$b),
                                     q = 3, alpha = 1, beta = 0), 2)
)
```

The house number separates `12 SMITH ST` from `21 SMITH ST` and from
`12A SMITH ST` in a way no similarity score will, and it says nothing at
all about the `PO BOX` and unit-number forms, where it is `NA` -- which is
the right answer, and why the comparison has to be *per component* rather
than one number for the whole line. `fsplit_field()`, `fextract()` and
`string_shape()` (@sec-uc-profile) are the tools for pulling the components
out; `freplace_tokens()` for the vocabulary.

## Cost is not the deciding factor

All nineteen comparators are compiled and parallel, so the choice can be
made on accuracy alone. On 200,000 pairs of surnames:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cost
#| tbl-cap: !expr sprintf("Seconds to score 200,000 pairs, %d cores, one run each (this machine -- yours will vary).", parallel::detectCores())
set.seed(1)
pool <- c("SMITH", "SMYTH", "JONES", "NGUYEN", "PAPADOPOULOS", "OBRIEN",
          "WILLIAMSON", "CHAUDHRY", "SZCZEPANSKI", "LEE")
left  <- sample(pool, 2e5, replace = TRUE)
right <- sample(pool, 2e5, replace = TRUE)
timings <- sapply(comparators, function(f) system.time(f(left, right))[["elapsed"]])
cost <- data.frame(comparator = names(timings), seconds = round(unname(timings), 3))
knitr::kable(cost[order(cost$seconds), ], row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Comparator", "Seconds"))
```

The spread between the cheapest and the dearest is a few hundredths of a
second over 200,000 pairs. Candidate generation, not scoring, is where a
linkage spends its time (@sec-benchmarks), so score two or three
comparators per field and keep the columns -- it costs almost nothing and
makes a clerical reviewer's job far easier than one blended number.

## What to use {#sec-recommendations}

| Field, and what goes wrong in it | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Given name**, typos and dropped letters | `osa_similarity()` | best AUC here; counts a transposition as one edit |
| **Given name**, where longer names are different people (`ALAN`/`ALANA`) | `osa_similarity()`, or `jaro_winkler(p = 0)` | length-sensitive; no prefix bonus to exploit |
| **Given name**, typos in the first letters | `jaro_winkler()` | the prefix bonus earns its keep |
| **Given name**, nicknames and short forms | `freplace_tokens()` first, then score | not a string-distance problem |
| **Given names** in one field, reordered | `jaro_winkler_tokens()`, `monge_elkan()` | align whole words in any order |
| **Surname**, taken down by ear | `editex_similarity()` | cheaper substitutions between like-sounding letters |
| **Surname**, general scoring | `osa_similarity()`, `lcs_seq_similarity()` | best AUC here |
| **Surname**, candidate generation | `soundex()`, `double_metaphone()`, `nysiis()` | perfect recall on easy and moderate pairs; far too generous to decide with |
| **Surname**, double-barrelled or added names | `tversky_index(alpha = 1, beta = 0)`, `fuzz_token_set_ratio()` | containment, ignoring what the other side adds |
| **Address**, whole-string comparison | `jaccard_index(q = 3)`, `cosine_similarity(q = 3)` | tolerant of token order, strict about unshared content |
| **Address**, one side carrying extra detail | `tversky_index(q = 3, alpha = 1, beta = 0)`, `smith_waterman()` | asymmetric: extra material in `b` is free |
| **Address**, reordered tokens | `fuzz_token_set_ratio()` | set comparison over words |
| **Address**, house number, unit, postcode | exact comparison of the parsed component | the decisive differences are one character long |
| Free text, long strings | `fuzz_token_set_ratio()`, `cosine_similarity()` | word sets, not character edits |
| You need to explain a score | `edit_ops()` | returns the edits themselves |

## Putting it together {#sec-recipe}

The four pairs below are the hardest kinds in this chapter: two different
people whose names look alike, and two matches disguised by a nickname and
by abbreviation. One comparator on one field cannot resolve them. The
recipe can: standardise, use the comparator that suits each field, compare
the decisive component exactly, and let the fields vote.

```{r}
#| label: recipe
left_file <- data.frame(
    given   = c("ALAN", "DANIEL", "MICHELLE", "ROBERT"),
    surname = c("BAKER", "THOMSON", "WILLIAMSON", "SMITH"),
    address = c("12 Smith St", "100 Queen St Brisbane",
                "7 Bottlebrush Crescent", "45 St Kilda Rd Melbourne"),
    truth   = c("different person", "different person",
                "same person", "same person")
)
right_file <- data.frame(
    given   = c("ALANA", "DANIEL", "MICHELE", "BOB"),
    surname = c("BARKER", "THOMPSON", "WILLIAMSEN", "SMYTH"),
    address = c("21 SMITH ST", "100 QUEEN ST MELBOURNE",
                "7 BOTTLEBRUSH CRES", "45 SAINT KILDA ROAD MELBOURNE")
)

std_name <- function(x) {
    freplace_tokens(fsquish(fupper(ascii_fold(x))), names(nicknames), nicknames)
}
prepare <- function(d) {
    d$given   <- std_name(d$given)
    d$address <- std_address(d$address)
    d$no      <- house_number(d$address)
    d
}
left_std  <- prepare(left_file)
right_std <- prepare(right_file)

scored <- rLink(
    left_std, right_std,
    pairs   = data.frame(x_index = 1:4, y_index = 1:4),
    compare = list(
        given   = osa_similarity(given),
        surname = editex_similarity(surname),
        address = tversky_index(address, q = 3, alpha = 1, beta = 0),
        number  = (function(x, y) as.numeric(!is.na(x) & !is.na(y) & x == y))(no)
    ),
    keep = c("given", "surname", "truth")
)
scored$decision <- ifelse(
    scored$number == 1 & pmin(scored$given, scored$surname, scored$address) >= 0.75,
    "match", "non-match"
)
scored[, c("given_1", "given_2", "surname_1", "surname_2",
           "given", "surname", "address", "number", "decision", "truth_1")]
```

All four land correctly, and each decision is readable: pair 1 is rejected
by the house number although every name score is respectable, pair 2 by the
locality inside the address score, and pair 4 is accepted only because
`BOB` became `ROBERT` before anything was compared. That is the shape to
aim for -- one column per piece of evidence, a rule you can state in a
sentence, and no single metric carrying the whole decision.

## Running this on your own data

The ranking in this chapter is the ranking for *these* pairs. Fields differ,
collection methods differ, and the only reliable way to choose is to grade a
few dozen pairs of your own and re-run the tables:

1. Take a sample of candidate pairs from your own blocking -- from
   `rLink()` with `compare = NULL`, say -- and label them, including the
   awkward ones. A hundred pairs per field is enough to separate the
   comparators; it is not enough to tune a threshold to three decimal
   places.
2. Grade each pair `easy`, `moderate` or `hard`, and keep the `kind` column.
   When a comparator does badly, the `kind` of the pairs it fails on tells
   you what to standardise.
3. Swap your data frame into `report()` above. Nothing else in the
   scaffolding is specific to these examples.
4. Read `margin` and the moderate columns, not the top line. A comparator
   with a high AUC and a thin margin is one bad batch of data away from
   failing.

@sec-uc-link puts the chosen comparators into a full linkage, and
@sec-theory explains what each one computes.
